subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 7-year-old girl has had 3 weeks of daily high spiking fevers that return to normal between spikes. She has a salmon-pink macular rash that appears with the fever spikes, and swelling of both knees and her right ankle. She is irritable and lethargic between episodes.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Kawasaki disease
Acute rheumatic fever

explanation_correct: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis occurs in children under 16 and presents with daily spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink macular rash, and arthritis in two or more joints. Anterior uveitis may be associated, and labs commonly show leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia, and elevated ESR and CRP. The quotidian fever pattern with rash and polyarthritis is classic.

explanation_incorrect.B: Oligoarticular JIA involves four or fewer joints and lacks the prominent daily spiking fevers and systemic rash seen here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause rash and arthralgia but the rash is malar and spares the nasolabial folds, and the disease is more typical in adolescent females with autoantibodies.
explanation_incorrect.D: Kawasaki disease features fever for more than 5 days with conjunctivitis, mucosal changes, cervical lymphadenopathy, and risk of coronary artery aneurysms, not this rash and arthritis pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acute rheumatic fever follows streptococcal infection with migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, and erythema marginatum rather than daily spiking fevers and a salmon-pink rash.

educationalObjective: Daily spiking fevers, a salmon-pink macular rash, and arthritis in multiple joints in a child younger than 16 indicate systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 9-year-old boy has daily spiking fevers and a salmon-pink macular rash with arthritis in three joints. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia, and markedly elevated ESR and CRP. Ophthalmologic examination reveals anterior uveitis. Rheumatoid factor is negative.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this disease?

options.text: It is strongly associated with HLA-B27 and rheumatoid factor positivity
The arthritis is typically symmetric and erosive, like adult rheumatoid arthritis
It most commonly presents after age 16 with a male predominance
The uveitis, when present, is typically posterior and granulomatous
It is a systemic arthritis of childhood with prominent acute-phase reactants and anterior uveitis

explanation_correct: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a systemic arthritis seen before age 16. It features daily spiking fevers, a salmon-pink macular rash, arthritis in two or more joints, and anterior uveitis, together with leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia, and elevated ESR and CRP. This combination of systemic inflammation, age, and anterior uveitis is characteristic.

explanation_incorrect.A: HLA-B27 and rheumatoid factor positivity are features of seronegative spondyloarthritis and adult rheumatoid arthritis, respectively, not systemic JIA.
explanation_incorrect.B: The arthritis of systemic JIA is generally not the symmetric erosive pattern of adult rheumatoid arthritis, and rheumatoid factor is typically negative.
explanation_incorrect.C: Systemic JIA is defined by onset before age 16 rather than after it, and it is not predominantly a disease of older adolescents.
explanation_incorrect.D: The associated uveitis is anterior, not posterior and granulomatous as in some other granulomatous diseases.

educationalObjective: Systemic JIA is a childhood systemic inflammatory arthritis with daily fevers, rash, elevated acute-phase reactants, and anterior uveitis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 52-year-old woman reports a gritty, sandy sensation in both eyes and dryness of her mouth for 6 months. She has difficulty swallowing dry food and a fissured tongue. Schirmer testing shows reduced tear production. Serologies are positive for anti-SS-A (Ro) and anti-SS-B (La), and rheumatoid factor is positive despite the absence of erosive joint disease.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus
Rheumatoid arthritis
Sjogren syndrome
Sarcoidosis
Graft-versus-host disease

explanation_correct: Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands, especially lacrimal and salivary glands, by lymphocytic infiltrates. It predominantly affects women aged 40 to 60 and causes keratoconjunctivitis sicca with a gritty eye sensation and xerostomia with fissuring of the tongue. Anti-SS-A (Ro) and anti-SS-B (La) are characteristic, and rheumatoid factor can be positive even without rheumatoid arthritis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Systemic lupus erythematosus has a malar rash, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies, and renal or neurologic involvement rather than isolated sicca symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.B: Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetric erosive arthritis; a positive rheumatoid factor alone in the absence of erosions does not establish it.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sarcoidosis features noncaseating granulomas and hilar lymphadenopathy and is not associated with anti-SS-A and anti-SS-B antibodies.
explanation_incorrect.E: Graft-versus-host disease occurs after hematopoietic stem cell or solid organ transplantation and is not a primary autoimmune exocrinopathy.

educationalObjective: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia, and anti-SS-A/SS-B antibodies in a middle-aged woman point to Sjogren syndrome.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing dry eyes and dry mouth develops progressive painless enlargement of the left parotid gland. She has multiple dental caries despite good oral hygiene. Biopsy of a labial salivary gland shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
question: Which of the following is the most important neoplastic complication she is at increased risk for?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma
Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Hodgkin lymphoma
Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid

explanation_correct: Sjogren syndrome carries an increased risk of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, which may present as progressive parotid enlargement. Other complications include dental caries from reduced saliva and an increased risk of giving birth to a child with neonatal lupus. Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis on labial salivary gland biopsy can confirm the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Oral squamous cell carcinoma is not the classic malignancy associated with Sjogren syndrome and is more strongly linked to tobacco and alcohol.
explanation_incorrect.C: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a salivary gland malignancy but is not the lymphoma risk emphasized in Sjogren syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hodgkin lymphoma is not a recognized complication of Sjogren syndrome; the associated lymphoid malignancy is of MALT type.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign mixed tumor of the parotid, not the malignant complication of chronic autoimmune sialadenitis.

educationalObjective: Sjogren syndrome predisposes to MALT lymphoma, which can present as enlarging parotid glands, and is diagnosed by focal lymphocytic sialadenitis on labial biopsy.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 34-year-old man presents with an acutely swollen, red, hot, and painful right knee with severe pain on passive movement and fever. Arthrocentesis yields purulent synovial fluid with 78,000 WBC/mm3, predominantly neutrophils. No crystals are identified, and Gram stain of the fluid is pending.
question: Which of the following is the most likely causative organism in this otherwise healthy adult?

options.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Staphylococcus aureus
Borrelia burgdorferi

explanation_correct: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the common causes of septic arthritis. This is typically monoarticular, with a swollen, red, painful joint and purulent synovial fluid containing more than 50,000 WBC/mm3. Untreated infection can lead to osteomyelitis, chronic pain, sepsis, and irreversible joint damage, so antibiotics with aspiration and drainage are required.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes disseminated gonococcal infection, often with tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and polyarthralgia in young sexually active patients rather than a single purulent joint in an unselected adult.
explanation_incorrect.B: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a less common cause of septic arthritis and is more typical in individuals with specific risks such as pneumococcal disease or asplenia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa osteomyelitis or arthritis is classically associated with plantar puncture wounds or intravenous drug use, neither of which is present here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme arthritis, which is generally not associated with purulent fluid containing more than 50,000 WBC/mm3.

educationalObjective: A monoarticular joint with purulent synovial fluid and more than 50,000 WBC/mm3 is septic arthritis, most commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever and a diffuse rash of small pustules on her extremities. She has pain and swelling in both wrists, and several extensor tendons on the dorsum of her hand are tender and swollen. She also reports dysuria, but no single joint contains overtly purulent fluid.
question: Which of the following best describes her condition?

options.text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis
Staphylococcal septic arthritis complicated by osteomyelitis
Reactive arthritis following a Chlamydia infection
Systemic lupus erythematosus with serositis
Acute gout involving the first MTP joint

explanation_correct: Disseminated gonococcal infection is a sexually transmitted infection that can present either as purulent arthritis, for example of the knee, or as a triad of polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis such as in the hand, and dermatitis with pustules. This patient's pustular rash, tenosynovitis, arthralgias, and dysuria in a sexually active young woman fit the triad pattern.

explanation_incorrect.B: Staphylococcal septic arthritis is typically a single swollen purulent joint rather than a diffuse pustular rash with tenosynovitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Reactive arthritis follows a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection and features conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis, not pustular dermatitis with tenosynovitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Systemic lupus erythematosus has malar rash, serositis, and autoantibodies, not a pustular rash with tenosynovitis and dysuria.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gout produces acute monoarthritis with needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals, not a pustular rash and tenosynovitis.

educationalObjective: Disseminated gonococcal infection may present with polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and pustular dermatitis rather than a single purulent joint.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: Four patients are evaluated for osteomyelitis: a 45-year-old with no underlying risk factors, a 62-year-old with an infected prosthetic hip, a 20-year-old with sickle cell disease, and a 30-year-old who developed infection in the foot after stepping on a nail through his shoe.
question: Which of the following correctly matches each patient's most likely causative organism?

options.text: Prosthetic joint: S aureus; sickle cell: Pseudomonas; plantar puncture: Salmonella
Overall: S epidermidis; prosthetic joint: Salmonella; sickle cell: S aureus
Overall: S aureus; prosthetic joint: S epidermidis; sickle cell: Salmonella; plantar puncture: Pseudomonas
Overall: Salmonella; sickle cell: S epidermidis; plantar puncture: S aureus
Overall: Pseudomonas; prosthetic joint: S aureus; sickle cell: S epidermidis

explanation_correct: The causative organism of osteomyelitis depends on the clinical setting. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common overall, Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic devices, Salmonella with sickle cell disease, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa with plantar puncture wounds. Matching the host factor to the organism is essential for choosing empiric therapy.

explanation_incorrect.A: This option misassigns Salmonella to a plantar puncture and Pseudomonas to sickle cell disease; the correct associations are the reverse.
explanation_incorrect.B: Staphylococcus epidermidis is linked to prosthetics rather than being the overall most common cause, and Salmonella is the sickle cell organism, not the prosthetic one.
explanation_incorrect.D: Salmonella is not the overall most common cause; it is specific to sickle cell disease, and S epidermidis is linked to prosthetic material rather than sickle cell disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pseudomonas is not the overall most common cause; it is specific to plantar puncture wounds, while sickle cell disease predisposes to Salmonella.

educationalObjective: Osteomyelitis etiology is host-specific: S aureus overall, S epidermidis with prosthetics, Salmonella in sickle cell disease, and Pseudomonas after plantar puncture.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Systemic JIA, Sjogren syndrome, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis
vignette: A 6-year-old develops fever, limping, and pain near the knee after a respiratory infection, and radiographs show bone destruction with periosteal elevation. A 58-year-old develops osteomyelitis at the site of recent orthopedic surgery. Both require imaging and microbiologic confirmation.
question: Which of the following best describes the typical spread and diagnosis of osteomyelitis in these patients?

options.text: Hematogenous spread is typical in adults and characteristically affects the metaphysis of long bones
Exogenous spread is typical in children and usually follows a plantar puncture wound
Diagnosis is best confirmed by serum uric acid measurement and polarized-light crystal analysis
Hematogenous osteomyelitis in children most often involves the epiphysis rather than the metaphysis
Hematogenous spread is typical in children, affecting the metaphysis of long bones; exogenous spread is typical in adults; diagnosis uses MRI and bone biopsy with cultures

explanation_correct: Osteomyelitis spreads hematogenously, usually in children where it affects the metaphysis of long bones, or exogenously, usually in adults after trauma, medical intervention, or spread from adjacent tissue. Common findings are pain, redness, swelling, fever, and limping. Diagnosis uses radiography showing bone destruction and periosteal elevation when chronic, MRI, and bone biopsy with cultures along with blood cultures.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hematogenous spread is characteristic of children, not adults, although the metaphyseal location is correct.
explanation_incorrect.B: Exogenous spread is characteristic of adults, particularly after trauma or surgery, rather than children.
explanation_incorrect.C: Uric acid and crystal analysis evaluate gout, not bone infection; osteomyelitis requires imaging and cultures.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hematogenous osteomyelitis in children classically involves the metaphysis of long bones, not the epiphysis.

educationalObjective: Childhood osteomyelitis is typically hematogenous and metaphyseal, adult disease is typically exogenous, and diagnosis relies on MRI and bone biopsy with cultures.
